t: 2760. Longest Even Odd Subarray With Threshold
o: Find the longest contiguous subarray that starts with an even number, strictly alternates parity, and never exceeds threshold. In [3,2,5,4] with threshold 5 the window [2,5,4] works (length 3); in [1,2] only [2] qualifies. With n ≤ 100 even an O(n²) scan passes, but a single left-to-right sweep achieves O(n): extend the current valid run while the alternation and threshold hold, otherwise restart at the next viable even element.
k: A valid subarray must begin at an even element ≤ threshold — restart points are exactly those indices.
Extend greedily while consecutive parities differ and every element ≤ threshold; the maximal run from each start is unique.
Single pass with a jump-over gives O(n); the run boundaries partition the array.

a.i: Scan i from left to right. When nums[i] is even and ≤ threshold, extend j while the next element is within threshold and of opposite parity to its predecessor; record j−i and continue from j. Otherwise skip i. Every maximal valid subarray is examined exactly once.
s: If nums[i] even and ≤ threshold: extend j while conditions hold; ans = max(ans, j−i); i = j.
a.t: O(n) — each index is visited a constant number of times across extensions and skips.

a.n: Approach 2: Brute force over all starts
a.i: For each even, in-threshold start l, extend r while valid and record lengths. O(n²) but trivially correct — good for sanity-checking the O(n) version.
s: Loop l over all indices passing the start condition.
a.t: O(n²) worst case — each start may scan to the array end.

w: Prefer the O(n) sweep; use brute force to validate. Pitfalls: a single element qualifies only if it is even and ≤ threshold (so [1,2] answers 1, not 2); when extension breaks on parity, jumping i to j (not j+1) is safe because nums[j] itself gets tested as a new start. Follow-up: what if the subarray must start odd, or the threshold applies only to the endpoints?
